newsitem.title: EGYPT: Small Egyptian investors join equities bandwagon.
newsitem.headline: Small Egyptian investors join equities bandwagon.

text.p: A mixed bag of eager investors queued outside National Bank of Egypt's branches and headquarters on Sunday in another sign of equity euphoria.

They were applying for shares in Egypt Cement, a new company planning to build a cement plant in the southern province of Qena, and their comments showed that despite years of state control they are already well-versed in equity analysis.

"The firm is near the New Valley project in Toshka and other construction projects in south Egypt, and this will cut transport costs," engineering student Haitham Sadeq told Reuters. He had been waiting three hours to submit his papers.
A 60-year-old man in the next queue said the price was cheap and had a good chance of going up. "And for the moment you pay only a quarter of the price," said the man, exporter Taha Jumaa.
With interest rates going down and share prices soaring, more and more Egyptians have moved their savings into equities.
The Capital Market Authority all-share index closed on Wednesday at a record 423.09 points, its 22nd highest level in a row and 41 percent above the level at the start of the year.
On Thursday, the market fell marginally in what brokers dubbed a healthy correction.
In the whole of 1996, the market rose 39.3 percent.
Analysts say large foreign inflows have been one of the main reasons behind the recent price leaps at the bourse.
Bank officials say a combination of factors has been behind the large demand for Egypt Cement.
"The people are encouraged by the cheap price, high share prices in general and increased public awareness," NBE investment manager Ibrahim Abdullah told Reuters.

The chairman of the Capital Market Authority, Abdelhamid Ibrahim, said in an interview earlier this month that investors would do better to put their money in new companies than in the existing listed companies.
But not all applicants had done their homework on Sunday.
"I was carrying a part of my savings to buy units in mutual funds, but when I found a crowd waiting here I decided to buy in Egypt Cement,"said one man, who refused to give his name.
The public offer to sell nine million shares in Egypt Cement (Qena) at 10.00 pounds ($3) each opened on February 16.
It will close after the statutory minimum period of ten days because it has already been covered, the agents said in a published announcement.
Applicants have said NBE had stopped taking applications. Abdullah denied this, but said the branches might have no forms.
Investors must apply for at least 25 shares, paying only one quarter of the face value plus an issuing fee of 0.10 pounds a share.
Another 25 percent of the share value is to be paid within six months of the date of establishment. The company will ask for the remaining half within a year.
$1 = 3.395 pounds
